title: Linear Neural Networks for Regression
oneLiner: Linear regression is a one-neuron network: weigh the inputs, add them up, and nudge the weights downhill until the predictions fit.

what.html:
Regression predicts a number (a price, a temperature) from input features. Linear regression assumes the number is a weighted sum of the features plus a constant: price ≈ w₀ + w₁ × size + w₂ × rooms.

Everyday versionA taxi fare: a fixed starting charge (the bias w₀) plus a rate per kilometre (w₁) plus a rate per minute waiting (w₂). Learning means discovering those rates from past receipts.

As a neural network, this is a single neuron: inputs times weights, summed, passed through the identity function (output = input), so it can produce any real number.

why.html:
• Many questions are "how much?": house prices, temperatures, energy use, salaries.
  • It's the simplest complete example of the deep-learning recipe: data, model, loss, gradient descent. Every bigger network reuses this loop.
  • The weights are readable: each one says how much the output changes per unit of that feature.

how.title: Organise the data as a table
how.html: Put each example in a row and each feature in a column, with an extra first column of 1s so the bias can be treated like any other weight. That table is the design matrix X; the answers form a column y; the weights form a column w. Then all predictions at once are just X times w.

how.title: One neuron, no squashing
how.html: The neuron multiplies each input by its weight and adds them up. For regression the activation is the identity: it passes the sum through unchanged, so predictions can be any number (not just 0/1) and the slope of the activation is always 1, which keeps the maths simple.

how.title: Score the predictions: squared error
how.html: For each example, take (prediction − answer)², halve it, and average over all examples. Squaring makes every error positive, punishes big misses much more than small ones, gives a smooth bowl-shaped loss with exactly one lowest point, and corresponds to assuming the noise is bell-shaped.

how.title: Walk downhill: gradient descent
how.html: The gradient says which way the loss goes up fastest; step the opposite way. For this model the gradient is simply "average of (error × input)". Repeat: predict, measure errors, compute the gradient, take a step of size η, until the gradient is tiny or you hit an iteration limit.

how.title: The learning rate
how.html: η is the step size. Too small and you crawl; too big and you overshoot the bottom of the bowl, bounce, and can blow up to infinity (NaN). The practical recipe: try 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, plot the loss curves, and keep the largest one that falls smoothly.

how.title: One step by hand
how.html: Sizes 1, 2, 3 with prices 2, 4, 5. Start with both weights at 0: every prediction is 0, loss = (4 + 16 + 25)/6 = 7.5. The errors (−2, −4, −5) give a gradient of (−3.67, −8.33); with η = 0.1 the weights become (0.367, 0.833) and the loss falls to 1.51, an 80% drop in one step.

how.title: Test on data the model hasn't seen
how.html: Fit on the training set, judge on a separate test set. Report errors in plain terms: MSE (average squared error), RMSE (its square root, in the target's units), MAE (average absolute error, less thrown by outliers) and R² (how much better than always guessing the average: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better, negative is worse).

how.title: Practical tips
how.html: Start weights at zero (fine for a single neuron). Build sensible features (price per square foot). Put features on similar scales (min–max to [0, 1], or subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation): otherwise one learning rate is too big for one feature and too small for another. Stop when the gradient or the loss change is tiny, or when validation loss starts to rise.

how.title: When it goes wrong
how.html: Loss is NaN → η too big or features unscaled. Loss bounces up and down → lower η. Loss doesn't move → η too small, or a sign error in the gradient/update. Great on training data but bad on test data → overfitting: fewer features, more data, or regularisation.

demo.html: Press Step once: you get exactly the numbers (gradient (−3.67, −8.33), new weights (0.367, 0.833), loss 1.51). Keep stepping or press Play to watch the line settle on the best fit. Then switch η to 0.4 and see it blow up.

example.html:
House price from size: the three-house example, solved one gradient step at a time. Salary from years of experience, crop yield from rainfall and fertiliser, energy use from temperature, hour and day are all linear regressions.

Supplementary In a mobile network, predict tomorrow's traffic volume per cell from today's traffic, the day of week and planned events; the weights show which factors drive load, and RMSE in GB tells planners how far to trust the forecast.

misunderstandings: Linear regression can only fit straight lines.
It's linear in the weights; add squared or other transformed features and it fits curves.
A bigger learning rate always trains faster.
Past a limit (here η ≈ 0.36) gradient descent overshoots and diverges.
Low training error means a good model.
Only error on unseen test data shows how well it generalises.
Feature scaling changes what the model can learn.
It doesn't change the best fit; it makes gradient descent reach it much faster.
takeaways: Regression predicts continuous values; linear regression uses ŷ = w₀ + w₁x₁ + … + w_dx_d.
It is one neuron with identity activation; in matrix form ŷ = Xw.
Squared-error (MSE) loss is smooth and convex with a single minimum.
Gradient descent: w ← w − (η/N)Xᵀ(Xw − y); η must be neither too small nor too large.
Scale features, evaluate on a test set with MSE/RMSE/MAE/R², and debug with loss curves.
thirty: Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of input features plus a bias, which is exactly a single neuron with an identity activation. We measure how wrong it is with the mean squared error, a smooth bowl-shaped loss with one minimum, and find the weights by gradient descent: compute the average of error times input, step the weights the opposite way scaled by the learning rate, and repeat. In the example one step cuts the loss from 7.5 to 1.51. In practice you scale features, pick a learning rate by plotting loss curves, stop when the gradient is tiny, and judge the model on a separate test set using RMSE, MAE or R².
